caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Paraguay is the region's low-debt anchor. The ratio fell from 21% of GDP in 2006 to a trough of 11.1% in 2011 on the soy and Itaipu boom, then rose gradually as governments borrowed for infrastructure: 15.6% in 2014, 18.6% in 2015, 25.8% in 2019, 36.9% in 2020 on COVID, 40.6% in 2022, a series high of 44.6% in 2024, and a projected 38.1% in 2025. The 2013 Fiscal Responsibility Law (deficit capped at 1.5% of GDP) kept the rise orderly, and the trajectory was rewarded: Moody's granted Paraguay investment grade (Baa3) in July 2024, with S&P following (BBB-) in December 2025. Dollar GDP grew from $13.4bn in 2006 to a projected $49.4bn in 2025. Debt sustainability is not the question here; the question is whether borrowing buys enough infrastructure to diversify beyond soy, beef, and electricity.
inflation_management: The Central Bank of Paraguay's inflation-targeting regime (adopted 2011, 4.5% target at the time, later 4%) has an unusually good record for a commodity exporter. Inflation hit 10.2% in 2008 on the food and fuel spike and 9.6% in 2006, then settled: 2.6% in 2009, 8.2% in 2011, and 2.7-5% through 2013-2020, including a low of 1.8% in 2020. The 2021-22 global shock pushed it to 4.8% in 2021 and 9.8% in 2022 - the drought-hit harvest amplified food prices - but the bank's tightening brought it back to 4.6% in 2023, 3.8% in 2024, and a projected 4.1% in 2025, essentially at target. Drought cycles remain the main inflation wildcard, but expectations are anchored and the floating exchange rate absorbs shocks.

key_events.event: Fernando Lugo's election ended 61 years of Colorado Party rule.
Lugo impeached; central bank adopted inflation targeting.
Horacio Cartes elected; Fiscal Responsibility Law capped deficits at 1.5% of GDP.
Commodity downturn and drought squeezed the soy-dependent economy.
Severe drought hit agriculture; COVID pushed debt to 36.9% of GDP.
Global commodity shock drove inflation to 9.8%, its highest in over a decade.
Santiago Pena elected (April); economy rebounded on a record harvest.
Moody's awarded investment grade (Baa3) in July 2024; S&P followed in Dec 2025; inflation projected at 4.1%.

outlook_next_decade: Paraguay's base case is the most boring in South America, and that is a compliment: inflation near target, debt near 38% of GDP, investment-grade ratings from two agencies, and steady 3.5-4% growth on agriculture, energy, and maquila manufacturing. Upside comes from Itaipu tariff renegotiation proceeds, green fertilizer and forestry investment, and deeper integration with Brazil and Argentina. The risks are climate (drought is a recurring GDP event, not a tail risk), commodity concentration, and whether the Fiscal Responsibility Law survives political pressure to spend the newfound credibility. Expect steady, not spectacular.
